vignette: Meet Agnes, a 79-year-old widow who spent her working life as a tailor. It's been decades since she served in the military, but the memories of that time still linger, haunting her every waking moment. The smell of blood, in particular, transports her back to the chaos of war. It's a scent that wafts from the fabric she works with, an occupational hazard that leaves her breathless and disoriented. As Agnes navigates her daily routine, certain conversation topics can trigger these unwanted thoughts. Friends and family, eager to reconnect, inadvertently push her buttons when they ask about her time in the service. Their queries are met with a stony silence or, worse still, an explosive outburst that leaves everyone stunned. These episodes have become so frequent that Agnes now avoids social gatherings altogether, preferring the solitude of her tailor's shop. But even there, memories of the traumatic event intrude upon her consciousness. The sequence of events remains hazy, and when she tries to recount them, words fail her. What she recalls most vividly is the rage that seizes her whenever those memories surface. Her hands, usually so skilled at crafting fine garments, now tremble with a mix of anger and despair. Over time, Agnes has come to believe that she's lost all sense of happiness. The optimism that once characterized her personality has given way to an oppressive emotional numbness. She feels dead inside, as if the trauma has extinguished some vital spark within her. When friends try to coax her out of this darkness, offering words of comfort or inviting her on outings, Agnes pushes them away, afraid that any positive emotions might make her vulnerable once more. Her memories of the event continue to plague her, influencing how she perceives her current circumstances. The trauma has convinced her that nothing good can happen to her anymore – a notion reinforced by every painful recollection. It's this sense of hopelessness that keeps Agnes stuck in a cycle of avoidance and maladaptive coping strategies. In an attempt to stave off these feelings, Agnes avoids situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful. She turns down invitations to family gatherings, declines offers from friends to join them for dinner, and generally withdraws from social interactions. These behaviors have consequences: her relationships begin to fray, and her isolation deepens. As Agnes reflects on her life, she realizes that the memories of the traumatic event continue to shape her perceptions and behavior. Her inability to put those memories in order or articulate them coherently only adds to her distress. The rage that accompanies recall has become a self-perpetuating cycle: each memory fuels more anger, which in turn reinforces her negative appraisals. In recent months, the weight of these memories has grown too much for Agnes to bear alone. Her shop, once a refuge, now feels like a prison – a constant reminder of the trauma she's desperate to escape. It's this desperation that brings her to therapy, hoping against hope that someone can help her unravel the tangled threads of her past and restore some semblance of happiness to her life.
